messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Bao was thirty-four when his body betrayed him. He was at his desk, refining a user flow for a new app, when a crushing weight settled on his chest. He remembers the wait for the ambulance feeling like an eternity, each tick of the clock a hammer blow of certainty that he would die right there in his home office. The diagnosis—a sudden, severe myocardial infarction—was a shock for a healthy, active man. He survived, but the man who came home from the hospital was not the same one who had been rushed there. The initial gratitude for his life quickly curdled into a persistent, gnawing question: why him? He had come to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with him, a hidden defect in his very makeup that had caused the attack and would surely strike again.

This conviction that he was a weak person, inherently flawed, has become the lens through which Bao now views the world. It has left him feeling profoundly unsafe in his own skin, his body a constant source of potential danger. He lives in a state of high alert, his muscles perpetually tense as if bracing for impact. His wife’s reassurances that the doctors fixed the problem and he is safe now are meaningless to him; he finds it impossible to believe her when his own body feels so hostile and untrustworthy. This unrelenting sense of physical threat only serves to confirm his deepest fear. A strong, healthy person wouldn’t live like this, he reasons, so the fact that he is constantly on edge must mean he is truly as weak and defective as he feels. The feeling of being perpetually on guard has also hollowed him out, leaving him with a sense of emotional numbness he describes as feeling "dead inside."

This pervasive sense of threat, fuelled by his negative self-appraisals, has systematically reshaped his life into a series of avoidant manoeuvres. To manage the terror of another medical emergency, he began to carefully excise any reminders from his daily existence. He cancelled his six-month cardiology follow-up, ignores the letters from the clinic, and feels a surge of panic at the sound of a distant ambulance siren. He has stopped all forms of exercise, terrified that putting his body under any physical stress might trigger a second, fatal attack. This avoidance is also fed by shame; he believes he is a weak person, and the thought of facing a doctor who might confirm this defectiveness is unbearable. He actively pushes away any thoughts about his time in the hospital, a mental flinching that has become as automatic as his physical avoidance.

The strategies meant to keep him safe have, over the past year, only tightened the cage of his anxiety. By refusing to get a physical examination, every minor chest twinge or bout of indigestion becomes a potential catastrophe with no expert voice to disprove it. By avoiding the gym, he never gets to experience his body as strong or capable, which leaves his perception of it as a fragile, failing machine completely unchallenged. This has made his work as a UX designer, once a source of pride, a new landscape of dread. When a prototype takes an extra few seconds to load, or a colleague is a minute late joining a video call, Bao feels a jolt of cold panic. He has come to believe that any delay, no matter how small, is a sign that something terrible is happening—a direct, visceral echo of the agonizing minutes he spent on the floor waiting for the paramedics to arrive.

The cumulative effect has created a chasm between him and his wife and left him feeling isolated and broken. He finally sought therapy after a severe panic attack at work, triggered by a delayed server response, left him hyperventilating in a bathroom stall, utterly convinced he was dying again. Bao’s stated hope is to feel normal, to trust his own body again, but he is terrified by the persistent thought that he is permanently damaged, that the weakness he perceives in himself is not a symptom of trauma but a fundamental truth he can never escape.
